lesson.title: Counting the Energy Cost of Chemical Change
lesson.summary: Enthalpy of reaction, delta H, is the signed heat exchanged with the surroundings at constant pressure when a reaction occurs exactly as its balanced equation describes.
lesson.body:
Every reaction rearranges bonds, and rearranging bonds costs or releases energy. Enthalpy of reaction, written delta H (or delta H rxn), is how chemists put a number on that energy exchange. It is defined as the heat absorbed or released at constant pressure, which is the normal condition for reactions happening in an open beaker or a living cell. Because enthalpy H is a state function, delta H depends only on the identity and amounts of the starting materials and final products, not on how the reaction actually proceeds. When delta H is negative, the products end up with less enthalpy than the reactants, and the difference leaves the system as heat: this is an exothermic reaction. When delta H is positive, the system absorbs heat from its surroundings to build higher-enthalpy products: this is endothermic.

A crucial detail that separates enthalpy of reaction from a vague notion of "how much energy a reaction releases" is that delta H is always reported for a specific balanced chemical equation with specific coefficients. The value -890.4 kJ for the combustion of methane means exactly one mole of CH4(g) reacting with two moles of O2(g) to give one mole of CO2(g) and two moles of liquid H2O. Change the coefficients, and you change the amount of heat, proportionally. This is exactly where stoichiometry enters: the balanced equation tells you the mole ratios, and those mole ratios tell you how delta H scales when you have more or less material than the textbook one-mole quantities. You cannot correctly use a thermochemical equation without first getting the stoichiometry right, and you cannot interpret a real quantity of heat released in a lab without converting your actual grams of reactant into moles.

That conversion, mass to moles to heat, is the standard calculation you will do constantly. Suppose the thermochemical equation is CH4(g) + 2 O2(g) -> CO2(g) + 2 H2O(l), delta H = -890.4 kJ, and you want to know how much heat is released by burning 4.00 g of methane. First convert mass to moles using the molar mass of CH4, which is about 12.01 + 4(1.008) = 16.04 g/mol: 4.00 g divided by 16.04 g/mol gives 0.2494 mol CH4. Since the thermochemical equation is written per one mole of CH4, you simply multiply: 0.2494 mol times -890.4 kJ/mol equals about -222 kJ. So burning 4.00 grams of methane, a little less than a teaspoon by mass, releases roughly 222 kJ of heat. Notice how the negative sign, the mole ratio from the balanced equation, and basic stoichiometric conversion all had to work together to get that answer.

This bookkeeping habit, always anchoring delta H to a specific balanced equation and using stoichiometry to scale it, is also what makes the next big idea possible. Because delta H is tied to a well-defined equation and is a property of a state function, you can add, subtract, reverse, and scale thermochemical equations like algebraic statements and trust that the resulting delta H is still physically meaningful. That is the foundation of Hess's law, which is where enthalpy of reaction becomes a genuinely powerful tool rather than just a labeled number.
